title: Interventions to Optimize Spinal Cord Perfusion in Patients With Acute Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: An Updated Systematic Review
condition_or_topic: Optimization of spinal cord perfusion after acute traumatic spinal cord injury
clinical_background: Ischemia and inadequate perfusion of neural tissue are considered important contributors to secondary injury after acute traumatic spinal cord injury. Hemodynamic management has traditionally focused on Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP). A guideline based on a 2013 systematic review issued a “Level III” recommendation to maintain MAP between 85 and 90 mmHg for the first 7 days after injury, but the neurological benefit of that target, the choice of vasopressor, and the duration of support remain uncertain. Interest has also grown in Spinal Cord Perfusion Pressure (SCPP), defined as the difference between MAP and either Intrathecal Pressure (ITP) or Intraspinal Pressure (ISP). There is no consensus on whether SCPP or MAP should guide hemodynamic management.
objectives: Update a systematic review published in 2020 to inform development of a clinical practice guideline for hemodynamic management after acute traumatic spinal cord injury.
Assess how goal-directed interventions to optimize spinal cord perfusion affect neurological recovery and adverse-event rates at any follow-up time.
Assess how monitoring techniques, perfusion ranges, pharmacological agents, and treatment durations affect neurological recovery and adverse-event rates at any follow-up time.
clinical_question: Patients: people with acute traumatic spinal cord injury. Interventions: goal-directed MAP or SCPP support, including particular monitoring techniques, perfusion ranges, pharmacological agents, and treatment durations. Comparators: any, including no intervention or alternative techniques, ranges, agents, or durations. Outcomes: extent of neurological recovery and rates of adverse events at any follow-up time.
study_design: Update of a systematic review published in 2020. The authors searched MEDLINE® (via PubMed®), EMBASE, The Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov for studies published from February 2019 to September 2021, and examined reference lists. Two reviewers independently assessed full-text eligibility and risk of bias, resolving disagreements by consensus.

population.description: Patients with acute traumatic spinal cord injury. The included evidence comprised one RCT and observational comparative studies, case series, and a case report.
inclusion_criteria: Acute traumatic spinal cord injury within 30 days of trauma.
A study of a goal-directed intervention to support or monitor spinal cord perfusion through MAP or SCPP, reporting neurological recovery or adverse events.
An RCT or observational study, including a comparative cohort, case-control study, case series, or case report.
exclusion_criteria: Studies reporting only intermediate or surrogate outcomes, without neurological outcomes or adverse events.
Unpublished studies, including conference proceedings and meeting abstracts.
Animal studies, editorials, letters, white papers, and narrative reviews.
Duplicate publications without distinct outcomes, single reports from multicenter trials, and preliminary reports superseded by later publications.

interventions: Goal-directed MAP support to optimize spinal cord perfusion.
SCPP support or monitoring, including measurement through intradural pressure probes at the injury site or lumbar intrathecal catheters.
CSF drainage through lumbar intrathecal catheters.
Different perfusion targets, monitoring techniques, pharmacological agents, and treatment durations.
comparators: Other monitoring techniques, perfusion ranges, pharmacological agents, or treatment durations.

primary: Extent of neurological recovery, including AIS grade, motor score, and Frankel grade.

statistical_methods: The authors planned a meta-analysis if appropriate and feasible, but clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded quantitative pooling; they therefore synthesized the findings qualitatively. They used GRADE to assess confidence in anticipated effects for each outcome, considering risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias.
follow_up: Eligible follow-up could occur at any time point. Across the included observational studies other than the case report, follow-up ranged from hospital discharge to 18 months post-injury; the RCT followed patients for six months post-injury.
quality_assessment_tool: Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tool for RCTs; Cochrane Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) for comparative observational studies; The National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool for noncomparative studies, supplemented with two domains from the Methodological Index for Nonrandomized Studies (MINORS) tool; and GRADE for confidence in the evidence.
interpretation: The updated review found only low or very low quality evidence about neurological recovery with MAP or SCPP support after acute traumatic SCI. The effect of MAP support remains uncertain, whereas higher SCPP may be associated with better neurological recovery. Either approach may entail specific adverse events, but their importance to patients has not been established. The evidence does not identify a well-supported monitoring technique, perfusion range, pharmacological agent, treatment duration, or overall hemodynamic protocol.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The update added nine studies to 19 from the previous review without resolving its principal uncertainties. The authors changed their description of the possible neurological benefit associated with higher SCPP from “appears likely” to “may be” to better reflect the very low quality evidence. Use of ROBINS-I produced a more critical risk-of-bias assessment than the earlier review’s MINORS assessment for some studies. As contextual evidence not included in this review, Torres-Espín et al suggested an intra-operative MAP range of 76 to 104-117 mmHg based on 118 patients, while Gee et al found that only 24% of MAP recordings from 16 patients fell between 85 and 90 mmHg. The authors also note that evidence informing several monitoring and pressure-threshold recommendations for severe traumatic brain injury is insufficient; those findings are not presented as evidence for SCI management.
clinical_implications: Avoiding hypotension and preserving spinal cord perfusion remain important principles in acute SCI care, although the reviewed literature does not provide high quality evidence for a particular protocol.
Low or very low quality evidence limits confidence in estimated benefits and harms, so strong recommendations may not be warranted and reasonable management may differ across clinical scenarios.
The relevance to patients of adverse events associated with perfusion interventions remains unclear because the included studies did not report patients’ views of those events.
practice_implications: The authors describe intensive monitoring and support of MAP and/or SCPP as potentially appropriate for an otherwise healthy young person with an isolated high-energy cervical fracture-dislocation and acute traumatic AIS B SCI; they also describe avoiding vasopressors or intensive care admission as potentially appropriate for a frail older person with severe preexisting cardiac dysfunction and a comparatively mild, possibly improving AIS D central cord syndrome after a low-energy fall. These are examples of how management could reasonably vary, not a specified protocol.

When developing guidance, the authors state that decisions should consider desirable and undesirable effects, confidence in effect estimates, typical patients’ values and preferences, resource use, acceptability, and feasibility.
limitations: The relevant literature provides low or very low quality evidence, limiting confidence in effect estimates and requiring caution when applying the findings to patient care.
Evidence quality for most outcomes was reduced by risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision.

Important limitations of included studies were the absence of direct intervention comparisons and inadequate control for selection bias, timing of surgery, other potentially useful co-interventions, timing of neurological examinations, and variation in injury level and neurological severity.
The included studies did not establish how important the reported adverse events were to patients.
strengths: The authors used rigorous methods to update the earlier systematic review and addressed clinical questions relevant to acute SCI management.

They searched multiple databases extensively, assessed primary-study risk of bias, considered clinical and methodological heterogeneity, sought reproducible study selection, reported in accordance with PRISMA, and used GRADE to assess confidence in anticipated effects.
open_questions: Whether MAP or SCPP support improves neurological recovery, and how their potential benefits compare with their harms, remains uncertain.
The evidence does not clearly establish which monitoring approach, perfusion range, vasopressor, or treatment duration should be used.
The importance to patients of adverse events such as a persistent CSF leak requiring another operation or an asymptomatic pseudomeningocele requiring no treatment remains unknown.
future_directions: Conduct prospective, controlled studies of interventions to optimize spinal cord perfusion after acute traumatic SCI, using objective, validated outcome assessments.
Investigate specific pharmacological agents used as vasopressors, an area for which the authors identify a continuing evidence gap.
Study the values and preferences of people with SCI, particularly their views on the adverse events associated with perfusion interventions.

main_findings.description: The updated search contributed new studies to the evidence base.
main_findings.value: 9 new studies; 19 studies from the prior review; 28 studies in total
main_findings.context: The updated search identified 569 potentially relevant citations. The included evidence comprised a single RCT and 27 observational citations.

main_findings.description: The effect of MAP support on neurological recovery remained uncertain.
main_findings.value: 16 observational studies; total n = 1109
main_findings.context: Evidence quality was very low. Most favorable evidence came from small uncontrolled studies, whereas two of the largest studies did not show a consistent benefit.

main_findings.description: In the Squair et al study, higher MAP was significantly associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade at 6 months.
main_findings.context: Prospective cohort of 92 patients; the implemented MAP goal was 80-85 mmHg for 5 days post-enrollment.

main_findings.description: In the same Squair et al study, higher SCPP was significantly associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade at 6 months.
main_findings.context: Prospective cohort of 92 patients. The publication's case-control analysis also reported OR 1.04, P < .01 for SCPP and improvement by at least one AIS grade.

main_findings.description: More frequent SCPP episodes below the threshold predicted a lower likelihood of AIS grade conversion in further analyses of the Squair et al cohort; the frequency of MAP episodes below its stated threshold did not.
main_findings.context: The SCPP threshold was 50 mmHg and the MAP threshold was 70 mmHg. Elsewhere, the review reports this SCPP finding as Odds Ratio (OR) .9, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.0, P = .03; these differently presented estimates are retained separately as reported.

main_findings.description: The separately reported Squair et al analysis associated SCPP episodes below 50 mmHg with failure to improve by at least one AIS grade at 6 months.
main_findings.context: The review's detailed account gives a differently presented interval and p value for an analysis of SCPP drops; the estimates have not been combined.

main_findings.description: In Martin et al, patients receiving vasopressors had significantly fewer hypotensive episodes, but motor score improvement did not differ significantly from that in patients not receiving vasopressors.
main_findings.value: 3.1 points with vasopressors vs 2.5 points without vasopressors
main_findings.context: Retrospective series of 105 patients; telemetry covered the first 72 h after admission. More frequent hypotensive events correlated with a need for vasopressors but not with motor scores at discharge.

main_findings.description: Higher SCPP may be associated with better neurological recovery, although the evidence does not establish the effect reliably.
main_findings.value: 8 observational studies (total n = 375); single RCT (n = 22)
main_findings.context: The observational evidence was very low quality and the RCT evidence was low quality. A multivariable analysis from a study sharing the ISCoPE dataset did not confirm the association.

main_findings.description: In the Kwon et al RCT, CSF drainage did not produce a statistically significant difference in motor score recovery compared with no drainage at 6 months.
main_findings.context: The RCT randomized 22 patients. The review also describes it as comprising 24 patients in its narrative discussion; the document gives both figures. It states that the trial was not powered to detect a neurological recovery difference.

main_findings.description: In Catapano et al, patients with AIS A injuries who improved by at least one AIS grade had higher MAP at discharge than those who did not improve.
main_findings.value: 96.6 vs 94.7 mmHg
main_findings.context: The study included n = 62; mean LOS was 40 days. Associations were also observed for AIS B and C, but not AIS D.

main_findings.description: In Chen et al, larger deviations from estimated optimal SCPP appeared to accompany poorer AIS grade recovery.
main_findings.metric: proportion improving by at least one AIS grade
main_findings.value: 30% with <5 mmHg deviation; 10% with 5-15 mmHg deviation; 0% with >15 mmHg deviation
main_findings.context: The reported outcome was at 9-12 months. The study did not find an association between MAP 85-95 mmHg and ASIA grade improvement.

main_findings.description: In adjusted analyses by Chen et al, greater intraspinal multi-scale entropy (MSE), but neither SCPP nor ISP, was significantly associated with improved neurological outcome.
main_findings.context: Mean follow-up was 17 months; MSE characterized the complexity of the ISP signal.

main_findings.description: In Cohn et al, more time at MAP ≤70 mmHg correlated with worse motor score recovery at discharge in unadjusted analyses.
main_findings.value: MAP ≤70 mmHg
main_findings.context: Uncontrolled retrospective series of n = 17.

main_findings.description: In Dakson et al, maintaining MAP ≥85 mmHg was associated with more frequent improvement by at least one AIS grade than having MAP <85 mmHg for at least 2 consecutive hours.
main_findings.metric: proportion improving by at least one AIS grade
main_findings.context: Mean follow-up was 27 days; n = 94.

main_findings.description: In Dakson et al, motor score improvement differed between the MAP groups described for AIS grade recovery.
main_findings.context: The first group maintained MAP ≥85 mmHg; the second had MAP <85 mmHg for at least 2 consecutive hours.

main_findings.description: In Ehsanian et al, more intraoperative time within the specified MAP range was associated with greater motor score change; MAP outside that range was not associated with motor recovery.
main_findings.metric: motor score increase per minute in range
main_findings.value: .036 for each minute at MAP 70-94 mmHg
main_findings.context: Retrospective series of n = 25; the association concerned the operative period.

main_findings.description: In Haldrup et al, the MAP threshold correlated significantly with long-term neurological outcome from the prehospital period through surgery and NICU days 1 and 2, but not NICU days 3-7.
main_findings.value: 80 mmHg
main_findings.context: Patients with MAP ≥80 mmHg had significantly better AIS improvement at 1-year follow-up than those with MAP <80 mmHg; n = 129.

main_findings.description: In Hogg et al, increasing SCPP across the reported range was linearly associated with motor score improvement, whereas values above that range were associated with lower motor scores.
main_findings.value: from <50 mmHg up to 110 mmHg; >110 mmHg
main_findings.context: Prospective uncontrolled series of n = 19 with AIS C injuries; SCPP goal ranges were not implemented.

main_findings.description: In the same Hogg et al series, increasing MAP across the reported range was associated with an average motor score gain.
main_findings.value: about 4 motor points with MAP increasing from <75 to 95 mmHg
main_findings.context: Prospective uncontrolled series of n = 19.

main_findings.description: In Hawryluk et al, higher mean MAP correlated with a higher rate of improvement by at least one AIS grade shortly after admission.
main_findings.context: Improvement was assessed within 3 days post-admission in n = 74. MAP readings <85 mmHg occurred less often among patients improving by at least one AIS grade within 7 days.

main_findings.description: In Levi et al, patients improved by at least one Frankel grade after treatment under the reported hemodynamic protocol.
main_findings.metric: proportion improving by at least one Frankel grade
main_findings.context: Assessment was at 6 weeks in an uncontrolled series of n = 50. Patients with motor-complete injuries and a persistently severe reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance index relative to systemic vascular resistance index appeared to have worse outcomes.

main_findings.description: In Park et al, mean MAP of at least 85 mmHg was not significantly associated with greater improvement by at least one AIS grade than the lower MAP categories.
main_findings.value: at least 85 mmHg vs 75-84 mmHg or <75 mmHg
main_findings.context: MAP was evaluated over the first 7 days after injury; AIS improvement was assessed at 3 months; N = 73.

main_findings.description: In Saadoun et al, higher SCPP was significantly associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade after adjustment for age and admission AIS grade.
main_findings.value: 2.7 with each SCPP increase of 10 mmHg
main_findings.context: Outcome was assessed at 9-12 months in n = 45.

main_findings.description: In a separate Saadoun et al model, lower ISP was significantly associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade; MAP did not correlate significantly with that improvement.
main_findings.value: 5.0 with each ISP decrease of 10 mmHg
main_findings.context: Outcome was assessed at 9-12 months in n = 45.

main_findings.description: In Sewell et al, introduction of a hemodynamic safety checklist was not associated with a difference in AIS score improvement or worsening.
main_findings.value: improved: 32% vs 27%; worse: 3% vs 2%
main_findings.context: The pre-checklist group had n = 38 and the post-checklist group n = 41; assessment was at 30 days. Low or very low MAP recordings were not associated with AIS score change in either cohort.

main_findings.description: In the Squair et al dataset, adherence to SCPP targets, rather than MAP targets, was the strongest reported indicator of neurological recovery.
main_findings.value: 60 to 65 mmHg
main_findings.context: The reported association concerned improvement by at least one AIS grade at 6 months; the related publications analyzed the same patient dataset. Clinical adherence and improvement were described as positively and linearly related.

main_findings.description: In Yue et al, patients improved by 1 AIS grade under a protocol targeting SCPP ≥65 mmHg; none worsened in AIS grade by discharge.
main_findings.context: Uncontrolled retrospective series of n = 15; discharge was on day 7 and the SCPP goal applied for 5 days.

main_findings.description: In Vale et al, improvement by at least one AIS grade was reported separately for patients admitted with AIS A and with AIS B, C, or D injuries.
main_findings.metric: proportion improving by at least one AIS grade
main_findings.value: AIS A: 3 (42%) among 31 patients; AIS B, C, or D: 24 (73%) among 33 patients
main_findings.context: Assessment was at 12 months. The document reports 3 (42%) among 31 patients with AIS A injuries; that apparent numerical inconsistency is retained without recalculation.

main_findings.description: In adjusted Weinberg et al analyses, a larger proportion of elevated MAP measurements was positively associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade.
main_findings.context: Each 10% increase in the proportion of elevated MAPs was described as associated with a 17% increase in AIS grade improvement. Measurements covered the first 72 hours after admission in n = 136. Vasopressor use was not associated with AIS grade improvement in adjusted analyses.

main_findings.description: In Werndle et al, higher SCPP shortly before examination correlated with higher total limb motor scores in the examined patients.
main_findings.context: The two correlations were reported among 2 patients with AIS C injuries, using SCPP from 30 minutes before examination within 7 days after injury; the document does not identify which coefficient belongs to which patient.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: For MAP support, very low-quality evidence from six observational studies (total n = 402) suggested that vasopressors may increase particular adverse events, although their importance to patients was unclear. Inoue et al reported adverse events in 74% of patients receiving vasopressors. For SCPP monitoring, the effect on adverse events was uncertain on the basis of 7 observational studies (n = 212) and a single RCT (n = 22).
safety_results.related_deaths: Vale et al reported no deaths associated with vasopressor use; a treatment-related death rate was not provided.
notable_adverse_events: Inoue et al reported cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial injury, acidosis, and skin necrosis among vasopressor-treated patients; adverse events occurred in 74%. Independent associations with adverse events were reported for dopamine (odds ratio [OR] 9.0, P < .01), phenylephrine (OR 5.9, P < .01), ≥ age 60 (OR 5.2, P = .01), and AIS A injury (OR 3.2, P = .03).

In the primary Readdy et al analysis of acute traumatic central cord syndrome, cardiac adverse events did not differ significantly between dopamine and phenylephrine (68% vs 45%, OR 2.5, P = .10). The reported events included atrial fibrillation, sinus and ventricular tachycardias, bradycardia, and troponin elevation.

In the other Readdy et al cohort, cardiac adverse events were significantly more frequent with dopamine (76%) than phenylephrine (40%) among patients with penetrating and blunt injuries (OR 4.7, P < .01). Events included atrial fibrillation, tachycardias, bradycardia, and troponin elevation. These Readdy et al studies appeared to have overlapping data.
In adjusted Weinberg et al analyses of n = 136, neither MAP values nor vasopressor use was associated with adverse-event risk; an event rate was not provided.
Vale et al reported no vasopressor-associated hypertensive hemorrhage, stroke, myocardial infarction, or death.
In the Kwon et al RCT, ITP monitoring and CSF drainage were not associated with increased adverse events; an event rate was not given.

Hogg et al reported asymptomatic pseudomeningocele on 6-week MRI in 46%, with all resolved by 1 year; CSF leakage around probes requiring re-suturing in 31%; blocked lumbar drains requiring removal or repositioning in 23%, 3/13; and wound infection in 8%, in the setting of brittle diabetes and E. coli bacteraemia from urosepsis.
In a Hogg et al series of n = 19, postoperative imaging showed asymptomatic pseudomeningocele in 21%, and CSF leakage from the probe site occurred in 11%, resolving after skin re-suturing.

In another Hogg et al series of n = 13, asymptomatic pseudomeningocele occurred in 54%. No other probe-related events, including cord damage, hematoma, CSF leakage, wound infection, or meningitis, and no other serious adverse events or reactions were reported.

Phang et al reported intradural pressure probe displacement in 2%, CSF leakage requiring revision of wound closure in 7%, and asymptomatic pseudomeningocele in 19%. No probe-related meningitis, surgical-site infection, hematoma, wound breakdown, or neurological deterioration was reported.
Squair et al reported no infectious or other complications arising from catheter placement; no rate was provided.
Werndle et al identified no adverse events related to intradural pressure probe placement; no rate was provided.
Yue et al reported no new neurological deficit or other complication related to LSAD placement; no rate was provided.

In the Zimering et al case report, postoperative apnea, unresponsiveness, facial myoclonus, and fixed downward deviation accompanied status epilepticus with a left posterior focus and bilateral occipital high T2 signal. Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) was diagnosed, and symptoms resolved rapidly after the MAP goals were stopped on postoperative day 2. The account reports several MAP measurements >100 mmHg without naming a specific vasopressor.

subgroup_analyses: Catapano et al observed MAP–outcome correlations in patients with AIS A, B, and C injuries, but not AIS D; among AIS A patients, MAP was 96.6 vs 94.7 mmHg for those who improved by at least one AIS grade versus those who did not (P < .01).
In Haldrup et al, the association involving the MAP threshold of 80 mmHg was significant during the prehospital period, surgery, and NICU days 1 and 2 (P ≤ .001 for all), but not on NICU days 3-7.

Among patients >55 years old in Readdy et al, cardiac adverse events were significantly more frequent with dopamine than phenylephrine (83% vs 50%, OR 5.0, P = .04), despite a non-significant difference in the primary analysis.

In Vale et al, the document reports improvement by at least one AIS grade at 12 months in 3 (42%) of 31 patients with AIS A injuries and 24 (73%) of 33 patients with AIS B, C, or D injuries. The AIS A count and percentage appear inconsistent within the document.
Werndle et al reported motor score correlations specifically among 2 patients with AIS C injuries: r = .65, P < .01 and r = .48, P < .05.
secondary_results: The updated search identified 569 potentially relevant new citations; 540 were excluded after duplicate removal or title and abstract review, and 20 after full-text review. It contributed 9 studies to 19 retained from the prior review, for 28 included studies. No new relevant trials were identified through ClinicalTrials.gov, and results remained unavailable for the four studies previously identified there.

Of 28 included citations, a single small RCT randomized 22 patients and 27 had observational designs: 11 comparative cohort or case-control studies, 15 case series, and one case report. Most assessed studies were rated poor quality (65%, 17/26). Three comparative studies were rated fair, while two case series were rated good; the review cautioned that case series cannot establish comparative effectiveness or safety.

The observational publications included potentially overlapping patient datasets: five retrospective studies from San Francisco General Hospital, eight analyses associated with ISCoPE (NCT02721615), and two analyses from a multicenter lumbar-catheter dataset. Consequently, counts of publications do not necessarily represent independent patient samples.
In the Kwon et al RCT, mean SCPP was higher with CSF drainage than without drainage (66 mmHg vs 59 mmHg, one-sided P = .04), although motor score recovery did not differ significantly at 6 months.

No study directly compared different specified MAP targets on patient-important outcomes. Table 6 describes Fifteen studies associating neurological recovery with MAP goals of 70-95 mmHg; the accompanying narrative calls them fourteen studies. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.

No study directly compared different specified SCPP target ranges on patient-important outcomes. Squair et al linked episodes below 50 mmHg to failure to improve by at least one AIS grade at 6 months (Odds Ratio (OR) .9, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.0, P = .03); a second analysis of the same dataset described 60-65 mmHg as the optimal adherence target. Yue et al associated SCPP ≥65 mmHg with AIS improvement in 15 patients, whereas Hogg et al associated SCPP >110 mmHg with reduced motor scores in 19 patients. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.

No study directly compared lumbar intrathecal catheter monitoring with injury-site ISP probe monitoring for patient-important outcomes. In a series of 13 patients undergoing both approaches, neurological outcomes were not reported; 4 required re-suturing around ISP probes for CSF leakage and 3 required lumbar catheter repositioning or removal because the catheters stopped working. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.

Three observational studies indirectly compared MAP support with SCPP or ITP monitoring within patient groups. Two analyses of the same dataset associated SCPP-target adherence, rather than MAP-target adherence, most strongly with AIS improvement at 6 months; SCPP drops below 50 mmHg, but not MAP drops below 70 mmHg or ITP drops below 29 mmHg, were associated with failure to improve. In the third study, SCPP, but not MAP, correlated significantly with neurological recovery at 9-12 months. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.

Three studies with apparently overlapping data associated dopamine with higher adverse-event rates than phenylephrine or other agents. One found no difference in neurological improvement between dopamine and phenylephrine. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.

No study directly compared different specified durations of MAP or SCPP support on patient-important outcomes. Fourteen studies reported associations involving MAP or SCPP goals over 3-7 days after injury. Evidence quality was VERY LOW.
In Phang et al, supine rather than lateral positioning was associated with higher ISP among patients who underwent laminectomy; the document does not give an effect estimate.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This systematic review updates Evaniew et al, J. Neurotrauma 2020. It examines whether support of Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) or Spinal Cord Perfusion Pressure (SCPP) affects neurological recovery or adverse events after acute traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI). Optimizing perfusion is considered important for limiting secondary ischemic injury, although the best approach remains disputed. The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE and ClinicalTrials.gov; two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted information and assessed bias. They used Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) to judge confidence in the evidence. Among 569 potentially relevant new citations since 2019, they added 9 studies to 19 from the earlier review, yielding 28 studies. Low or very low quality evidence leaves the neurological effect of MAP support uncertain and suggests that greater SCPP may improve neurological recovery. Both approaches may carry specific adverse-event risks, whose importance to patients is unclear. Very low quality evidence cannot reliably identify preferred monitoring methods, perfusion ranges, drugs or treatment durations. The review informs a new clinical practice guideline, but the literature does not provide high quality support for a particular hemodynamic protocol. Avoiding hypotension and maintaining spinal cord perfusion remain important principles; prospective controlled studies with objective, validated outcomes are needed.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Neural ischemia and hypoperfusion are considered important contributors to secondary injury after acute traumatic SCI. Perfusion-directed care is thought to matter, but its details remain contested. Hemodynamic care has traditionally emphasized MAP. A guideline arising from a 2013 systematic review gave a “Level III” recommendation to maintain MAP between 85 and 90 mmHg for the first 7 days after injury. The neurological value of that target for every patient, the best vasopressor and the appropriate duration remain uncertain. Research on blood pressure and spinal cord perfusion has expanded during the last decade. Interest has also grown in SCPP, defined as MAP minus either Intrathecal Pressure (ITP) or Intraspinal Pressure (ISP); there is no consensus on whether SCPP or MAP should guide hemodynamic care. Further evidence synthesis is needed to support decisions, improve individual neurological outcomes and limit adverse events. Clinical practice guidelines aim to improve care through recommendations. Trustworthy guidelines require rigorous development and current, comprehensive systematic reviews that address both benefits and harms and the quality of evidence. To inform a new guideline, the authors updated a review published in 2020. Their questions concern the effects of perfusion-directed interventions on neurological recovery and adverse events at any follow-up, and the corresponding effects of specific monitoring methods, perfusion ranges, drugs and treatment durations.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors revisited the earlier review’s rationale, questions, eligibility criteria and procedures using published guidance for updating systematic reviews. They followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Methods Guide, and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement. Because this was a systematic review, informed consent and institutional review board approval were unnecessary.

document_sections.heading: Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
document_sections.content: Eligibility was specified in advance by population, intervention, comparator, outcome, timing and study design, as set out in Table 1. Eligible patients had acute traumatic SCI within 30 days of trauma; chronic SCI and other diagnoses were excluded. Eligible interventions intentionally supported or monitored spinal cord perfusion through MAP or SCPP, with any comparator, including no intervention. Comparisons of monitoring methods, perfusion ranges, drugs or treatment durations were also eligible. Critical outcomes were neurological recovery, including AIS grade, motor score or Frankel grade, and adverse-event rates; HRQOL and cost-effectiveness were noncritical outcomes. Follow-up could occur at any time. RCTs and observational designs, including comparative cohorts, case-control studies, case series and case reports, were eligible. Studies reporting only physiological or other intermediate outcomes without neurological outcomes or adverse events were excluded, as were animal studies, abstracts, editorials, letters, specified duplicate or preliminary publications, single reports from multicenter trials, white papers, narrative reviews and meeting proceedings. Unlike the earlier review, this update excluded unpublished studies, including conference proceedings, because their risk of bias could not be fully assessed.

document_sections.heading: Electronic Literature Search and Study Selection
document_sections.content: To find studies published after the earlier review, the authors searched MEDLINE® via PubMed®, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library and ClinicalTrials.gov from February 2019 to September 2021. They also examined references in included articles and relevant systematic reviews. Two team members screened potentially eligible titles and abstracts against established criteria. Any citation considered potentially relevant by at least one reviewer proceeded to full-text assessment; a second reviewer checked exclusions made before that stage. Two reviewers independently assessed full-text eligibility and settled disagreements by consensus.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction
document_sections.content: Using the earlier review’s template, the authors collected patient, study, surgical, adjunctive-treatment and intervention characteristics, together with neurological and adverse-event outcomes. One team member extracted each study’s data and another checked completeness and accuracy. For RCTs, they assessed bias with the Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tool; for comparative observational studies, with the Cochrane Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool; and for noncomparative studies, with The National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool. Observational assessments also incorporated two Methodological Index for Nonrandomized Studies (MINORS) domains covering blinded outcome assessment and follow-up losses. Two reviewers independently rated each study, resolved differences by consensus and reassessed previously included studies using these tools. Table 2 defines the “good,” “fair,” and “poor” ratings.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis
document_sections.content: The authors had planned meta-analysis if suitable, but substantial clinical and methodological differences again prevented quantitative pooling; they therefore synthesized findings qualitatively. They applied Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) to anticipated effects for each outcome and revised earlier ratings where new evidence was available. RCT evidence began as high quality and could be downgraded for bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness or publication bias. Observational evidence began as low quality and could be downgraded on the same grounds or upgraded for a large effect, a dose–response pattern or biases unlikely to overturn the conclusion. Imprecision was assigned when estimates rested on few uncontrolled studies, controlled studies could not rule out benefit or harm, or the combined sample would lack adequate power for the observed estimate. Conflicting results among similarly sized or designed studies prompted downgrading for inconsistency. Studies linking outcomes to perfusion measurements without comparing active perfusion interventions against controls prompted downgrading for indirectness. One author initially formulated the ratings; all authors reviewed and agreed on them.

document_sections.heading: Results Study Selection
document_sections.content: The updated search found 569 potentially relevant citations. Duplicate removal or title and abstract screening excluded 540, and full-text assessment excluded another 20. The remaining nine new studies joined 19 from the earlier review, for 28 included studies of perfusion optimization after acute traumatic SCI. Figure 1 depicts selection, and Table 4 describes the included studies. Across the searches, the usual full-text exclusion reasons were failure to evaluate a perfusion intervention or to report an outcome of interest. ClinicalTrials.gov supplied no new relevant trials, and results were still unavailable for the four studies identified there by the earlier review. The update also removed two previously included abstracts because the underlying studies remained unpublished.

document_sections.heading: Overview of Included Studies
document_sections.content: Among the 28 citations, one small RCT from the earlier review randomized 22 patients to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage targeting ITP of 10 mmHg or to no drainage, with six months of follow-up. Mean age was 41 years, 68% were male, 77% had cervical injuries and 55% had ASIA impairment scale (AIS) grade A injuries. The other 27 citations were observational: 11 comparative cohort or case-control studies, including four new ones; 15 case series, including five new ones; and one previously included case report. Apart from the case report, observational samples ranged from 13 to 136, mean ages from 32 to 62 years, male proportions from 61 to 100%, cervical-injury proportions from 39% to 100%, and AIS A proportions from 0 to 100%. Most excluded penetrating injury or did not state whether it occurred; most did not report corticosteroid use. Follow-up extended from hospital discharge to 18 months after injury. Most studies, 65%, 17/26, were rated poor, chiefly because of possible selection bias and unclear follow-up losses. The best comparative-study rating was fair, achieved by three studies. Two case series were rated good, but their inability to establish comparative effectiveness or safety and their other limitations warrant caution. Three groups of observational articles appeared to draw on overlapping data; the authors listed articles separately but downgraded confidence for imprecision where apparent combined sample sizes contained repeat publications. Five retrospective studies used admissions to the Neurotrauma Intensive Care Unit at San Francisco General Hospital between 2005 and 2011. Eight studies, three new, analyzed the ongoing prospective Injured Spinal Cord Pressure Evaluation (ISCoPE) study (NCT02721615), which uses intradural probes at the injury site to calculate SCPP. Two studies, one new, separately analyzed the same multicenter dataset in which lumbar intrathecal and standard arterial catheters measured CSF pressure and MAP for SCPP calculation.

document_sections.heading: Effects of Interventions to Optimize Spinal Cord Perfusion
document_sections.content: Table 5 summarizes neurological and adverse-event findings for perfusion-directed interventions. Table 6 summarizes findings concerning monitoring techniques, target ranges, drugs and treatment durations.

document_sections.heading: KQ1: In patients with acute traumatic spinal cord injuries, what are the effects of goal-directed interventions to optimize spinal cord perfusion on extent of neurological recovery and rates of adverse events at any time point of follow-up?
document_sections.content: This question addresses neurological recovery and adverse events at any follow-up after interventions intended to optimize perfusion in acute traumatic SCI.

document_sections.heading: The Effects of MAP Support on Neurological Recovery.
document_sections.content: Five new studies joined 11 earlier studies. Across 16 observational studies (total n = 1109), very low quality evidence leaves the neurological effect of MAP support uncertain. Evidence favoring support mostly comes from small uncontrolled studies, while two of the largest did not show consistent benefit. Study design, bias, indirectness and inconsistency reduced confidence. In a prospective cohort of 92 patients, Squair et al inserted lumbar ITP catheters within 48 h of injury for up to one week and pursued MAP of 80-85 mmHg for 5 days after enrollment. At 6 months, both MAP (Odds Ratio (OR) 1.04, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.06, P < .01) and SCPP (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.06, P < .01) were significantly associated with improvement by at least one AIS grade. More frequent SCPP falls below 50 mmHg significantly predicted a lower likelihood of conversion (OR .9, 95% CI 0.81 to .98, P < .05); more frequent MAP falls below 70 mmHg did not. Martin et al retrospectively analyzed 105 patients’ telemetry during the first 72 h after admission to estimate hourly minimum and average MAP, mean MAP and hypotensive-event frequency. More hypotensive events correlated with vasopressor need, but not with motor scores at discharge.

document_sections.heading: The Effects of MAP Support on Adverse Events.
document_sections.content: One new study joined five earlier studies; two previously included unpublished abstracts were removed. Six observational studies (total n = 402) provide very low quality evidence that vasopressors used for MAP support may increase adverse events, including arrhythmias, myocardial injury, acidosis and skin necrosis. The most informative cardiac-risk estimates came from two studies with overlapping data: retrospective reviews of 36 patients with AIS A injury and 34 patients with acute traumatic central cord syndrome. Both used dopamine and/or phenylephrine to maintain MAP >85 mmHg for a mean of 4 days. Cardiac-event rates ranged from 40% with phenylephrine to 76% with dopamine; tachycardias, atrial fibrillation, elevated troponin and bradycardia were common. Their importance to patients was not reported and remains unclear. A newer retrospective study of 136 patients with AIS A to D injuries used various vasopressors as needed to maintain MAP ≥85 mmHg during the first 72 hours of admission and did not identify an association between vasopressor use and adverse events. Study design, bias, indirectness and inconsistency lowered confidence to very low.

document_sections.heading: The Effects of SCPP Support on Neurological Recovery.
document_sections.content: Three new studies joined six earlier studies. Eight observational studies (total n = 375) provide very low quality evidence, and the single RCT (n = 22) provides low quality evidence, that greater SCPP may be associated with improved neurological recovery. Squair et al (n = 92) found a statistically significant association with improvement by at least one AIS grade through six months; two uncontrolled studies drawing on the same ISCoPE data (n = 45 in each) found such an association through 12 months. Another ISCoPE analysis with mean follow-up of 17 months did not confirm the association after multivariable adjustment. In the RCT, lumbar-catheter CSF drainage was not associated with better neurological recovery. The article also describes that safety and feasibility trial as comprising 24 patients and lacking power to detect a neurological difference, whereas its study overview and evidence summary report n = 22. The authors changed their description of the SCPP association from “appears likely” to “may be” to reflect uncertainty. Study design, bias, indirectness, inconsistency and imprecision lowered confidence.

document_sections.heading: The Effects of SCPP Support on Adverse Events.
document_sections.content: Four new studies joined four earlier studies. Seven observational studies (n = 212) provide very low quality evidence and the single RCT (n = 22) low quality evidence; the adverse-event effect of SCPP monitoring remains uncertain. In two ISCoPE studies, CSF leakage requiring skin re-suturing occurred in 7%11% of patients, as rendered in the prose; no probe-related surgical-site infection, hematoma, wound breakdown, meningitis or neurological deterioration was reported. The importance of re-suturing to patients was not reported and is unclear. Asymptomatic pseudomeningocele occurred in 7/13 (54%) ISCoPE patients whose intrathecal catheter was inserted intra-operatively at the injury site. Study design, bias, indirectness, inconsistency and imprecision reduced confidence.

document_sections.heading: KQ2: In patients with acute traumatic spinal cord injuries, what are the effects of particular monitoring techniques, perfusion ranges, pharmacological agents, and durations of treatment on extent of neurological recovery and rates of adverse events at any time point of follow-up?
document_sections.content: This question addresses whether specific monitoring approaches, perfusion targets, pharmacological agents or treatment durations affect neurological recovery and adverse events at any follow-up in acute traumatic SCI.

document_sections.heading: MAP Goal Ranges.
document_sections.content: Five new studies joined ten from the earlier review. None directly compared specific MAP targets for patient-important outcomes. The text says fourteen studies described associations between neurological recovery and MAP targets of 70-95 mmHg, whereas Table 6 says Fifteen studies. Study design, bias and indirectness reduced evidence quality to very low.

document_sections.heading: SCPP Goal Ranges.
document_sections.content: Three new studies joined one earlier study. No study directly compared specific SCPP ranges for patient-important outcomes. In Squair et al, episodes below 50 mmHg were associated with failure to improve by at least one AIS grade at six months (Odds Ratio (OR) .9, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.0, P = .03); a secondary analysis of the same data identified adherence to 60-65 mmHg targets as optimal. In Yue et al’s observational study of 15 patients, SCPP equal to or greater than 65 mmHg was associated with AIS-grade improvement. In an ISCoPE series of 19 patients, SCPP greater than 110 mmHg was associated with lower motor scores. Study design, bias, indirectness and imprecision reduced confidence to very low.

document_sections.heading: SCPP Techniques.
document_sections.content: The article describes two ways to estimate SCPP. One places a subdural pressure sensor at the injured site during surgery; pressure from the swollen cord against the dura provides ISP, and SCPP equals MAP minus ISP. The other places a lumbar intrathecal catheter below the injury to measure ITP; CSF can be drained to increase SCPP, calculated as MAP minus ITP. The latter is the established approach during thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm surgery. Lumbar ITP may not represent pressure at the injury if swelling compresses the cord against the thecal sac and blocks the subarachnoid space. One new ISCoPE series of 13 patients simultaneously measured lumbar CSF pressure and injury-site ISP; the earlier review had no such study. It reported no neurological outcomes. Four patients required re-suturing around ISP probes for CSF leakage, and three required lumbar-catheter removal or repositioning after catheter failure. Study design, bias, indirectness and imprecision reduced the evidence to very low quality.

document_sections.heading: MAP vs SCPP Goals.
document_sections.content: One new study joined two earlier observational studies. All three made indirect within-group comparisons between MAP support and monitoring of SCPP or ITP. Two analyses of Squair et al’s dataset linked adherence to SCPP targets, rather than MAP targets, most strongly with improvement by at least one AIS grade at six months. SCPP falls below 50 mmHg were associated with failure to improve, whereas MAP falls below 70 mmHg and ITP falls below 29 mmHg were not. In a third study of 45 ISCoPE patients, SCPP, but not MAP, correlated significantly with neurological recovery at 9-12 months. Study design, bias, indirectness and imprecision reduced confidence to very low.

document_sections.heading: Choice of Vasopressor.
document_sections.content: No new study met inclusion criteria, and an earlier unpublished abstract was removed. Three studies that apparently shared overlapping data compared drugs for MAP support. Each associated dopamine with more adverse events than phenylephrine or other agents. One found no difference in neurological improvement between dopamine and phenylephrine recipients. Study design, bias, indirectness and imprecision reduced evidence quality to very low.

document_sections.heading: Duration of Treatment.
document_sections.content: The authors added four new studies, nine earlier studies and one earlier study not previously assessed for this question because the former review considered only MAP-support duration, whereas this update also considered SCPP. None directly compared treatment durations for patient-important outcomes. Fourteen included studies reported associations between neurological recovery and MAP or SCPP targets maintained for 3-7 days after injury. Study design, bias, indirectness and imprecision reduced evidence quality to very low.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: This update was intended to inform a clinical guideline on perfusion optimization after acute traumatic SCI. Nine new studies joined 19 earlier studies. As before, only low or very low quality evidence addresses neurological recovery with MAP or SCPP support. Very low quality evidence suggests that either approach may involve particular adverse events, but studies did not report their importance to patients. It provides no clear choice of monitoring technique, perfusion range, drug or treatment duration. The authors identify rigorous updating methods as the principal strength: clinically relevant questions, extensive database searches, primary-study bias assessment, attention to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, reproducible selection, reporting in line with PRISMA and GRADE assessment of confidence.

document_sections.heading: Discussion — limitations and context
document_sections.content: The main limitation is the low or very low quality of the available studies, which limits confidence in effects and calls for caution when applying findings to care. Most outcome ratings were lowered for bias, indirectness, inconsistency or imprecision. Primary-study weaknesses included lack of direct intervention comparisons and inadequate control for selection bias, surgery timing, other potentially useful co-interventions, neurological-examination timing, injury level and neurological severity. For context, the 2016 Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines found evidence insufficient for a “Level I” recommendation on Intracranial Pressure (ICP) monitoring, Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) monitoring, advanced cerebral monitoring or specific Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP), ICP and CPP thresholds. An RCT of 324 patients found no outcome difference with versus without ICP-monitor information, whereas four observational studies (total n = 13,164) suggested an association between ICP monitoring and lower in-hospital and 2-week mortality. This update used ROBINS-I and The National Institutes of Health tool for observational studies; the earlier review had used MINORs for all such studies. ROBINS-I assessed some studies more critically and led to additional downgrading for bias on some outcomes. Assessing bias in observational work is especially contested because varied methodological features can produce misleading results. MINORS has acceptable psychometric properties and has been validated to identify excellent observational studies, but ROBINS-I is preferred by the Cochrane Collaboration; it assesses specific results through bias domains, guiding questions and an overall judgment.

document_sections.heading: Discussion — subsequently published studies
document_sections.content: Relevant research continued after the search and was not included in the update. Torres-Esp´ın et al applied machine learning to continuous intra-operative MAP measurements from 118 surgical patients with acute traumatic SCI. They suggested maintaining MAP between 76 and 104-117 mmHg and emphasized avoiding excessive hypertension as well as hypotension. Gee et al examined continuous MAP measurements during the first five days in intensive care for 16 patients and found only 24% of recordings between 85 and 90 mmHg. They argued that maintaining MAP within a 5 mmHg band is very difficult in practice and characterized adherence to such guidance as ‘almost impossible’.

document_sections.heading: Implications
document_sections.content: Together with the earlier review, this update supplies evidence for developing a new guideline on acute hemodynamic care after traumatic SCI. Low or very low quality evidence across the outcomes suggests that strong recommendations may be unwarranted and that reasonable care may differ by clinical circumstances. The authors illustrate that intensive MAP and/or SCPP monitoring and support might be appropriate for an otherwise healthy young patient with an isolated high-energy cervical fracture-dislocation and acute AIS B SCI, while avoiding vasopressors or intensive care admission might also be appropriate for a frail older patient with substantial preexisting cardiac dysfunction and comparatively mild, possibly improving AIS D central cord syndrome after a low-energy fall. These are examples of context-dependent decisions, not established treatment effects. Under the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework, recommendation direction and strength also depend on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, confidence in effect estimates, typical patients’ values and preferences, resources, acceptability and feasibility. Strong recommendations are rarely appropriate with low or very low quality evidence. Further high quality research could resolve uncertainty and improve confidence and care. Acute traumatic SCI trials are difficult because of logistics, acuity, time sensitivity and patient heterogeneity, although included studies show that reliable research is possible. Evidence offers no clear choice of vasopressor drug, an important gap. A prospective cohort of 11 patients suggesting that norepinephrine maintained MAP with lower ITP and consequently higher SCPP than dopamine was excluded because it reported neither neurological recovery nor adverse events. A non-human porcine study suggesting better spinal cord blood flow and oxygenation with norepinephrine than phenylephrine was also excluded. Evidence extrapolated from traumatic brain injury is limited: a recent systematic review found only two observational drug-comparison studies, neither identifying a significant between-group difference, and the Brain Trauma guidelines did not recommend a particular drug. Research into SCI patients’ values and preferences is also needed, particularly how they view identified adverse events. Patients may regard an operation for persistent CSF leakage after intradural-catheter placement differently from an untreated, asymptomatic pseudomeningocele.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The update supports development of a new guideline for hemodynamic management after acute traumatic SCI. Avoidance of hypotension and maintenance of spinal cord perfusion are important principles, but available research offers no high quality evidence favoring a particular protocol. Further prospective controlled studies using objective, validated outcome measures are required to evaluate perfusion-optimizing interventions.

tables.title: Table 6. Summary of Findings: Techniques of Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Spinal Cord Perfusion Pressure (SCPP) Support.

rows: MAP goal ranges
No study directly compared particular MAP targets on patient-important outcomes. Fifteen studies examined associations between neurological recovery and MAP goals of 70-95 mmHg.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness.
SCPP goal ranges

No direct comparison of particular SCPP ranges on patient-important outcomes was available. In an observational dataset, SCPP episodes below 50 mmHg were associated with failure to gain at least one AIS grade at 6 months (Odds Ratio (OR) .9, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.0, P = .03); another analysis of the same dataset favored adherence to 60-65 mmHg. One study of 15 patients linked SCPP ≥65 mmHg with AIS improvement, whereas one study of 19 patients linked SCPP >110 mmHg with reduced motor scores.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision.
SCPP techniques

No study directly compared lumbar intrathecal catheters with injury-level ISP probes for patient-important outcomes. A study of 13 patients monitored both pressures without reporting neurological outcomes; 4 patients needed ISP-probe-site re-suturing for CSF leakage, and 3 needed lumbar-catheter repositioning or removal after catheter failure.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision.
MAP vs SCPP goals

Three observational studies made indirect within-group comparisons. Two analyses of one dataset associated adherence to SCPP, rather than MAP, targets most strongly with gain of at least one AIS grade at 6 months; SCPP drops below 50 mmHg, but not MAP drops below 70 mmHg or ITP drops below 29 mmHg, were associated with failure to improve. A third study associated SCPP and decreased ITP, but not MAP, with recovery at 9-12 months.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision.
Choice of vasopressor

Three studies with apparently overlapping data associated dopamine with more AEs than phenylephrine or other agents; one reported no neurological-improvement difference between dopamine and phenylephrine.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision.
Duration of treatment

No study directly compared particular MAP- or SCPP-support durations on patient-important outcomes. Fourteen studies examined associations between neurological recovery and MAP or SCPP goals applied for 3-7 days after injury.
VERY LOW; study design, risk of bias, indirectness, imprecision.

main_conclusion: This updated review offers evidence for developing guidance on acute traumatic SCI hemodynamic care, but it does not establish a particular protocol with high-quality evidence. The authors consider avoiding hypotension and preserving spinal cord perfusion important principles and call for prospective controlled studies using validated, objective outcomes.
narrative_summary: This systematic review update assessed whether MAP or SCPP support improves neurological recovery or affects adverse-event rates after acute traumatic SCI. Searches identified 9 new studies, combined with 19 from the previous review for 28 studies overall; substantial clinical and methodological differences prevented meta-analysis. The evidence included one small RCT and predominantly observational studies, many rated poor quality. Across 16 observational studies (total n = 1109), the neurological effect of MAP support remained uncertain. Evidence from eight observational studies (total n = 375) suggested that higher SCPP may be associated with better neurological recovery, although findings were inconsistent; the RCT (n = 22) did not show improved neurological recovery with CSF drainage. Vasopressor-based MAP support may carry risks including cardiac events, while SCPP-monitoring procedures were associated with complications such as CSF leakage and asymptomatic pseudomeningocele. The importance of these events to patients remains unclear. No direct evidence established a preferred MAP or SCPP range, monitoring technique, pharmacological agent, or treatment duration. Confidence in the relevant findings was LOW or VERY LOW, in part because of bias, indirect comparisons, inconsistency, and imprecision. For clinical guidance, the authors emphasize that avoiding hypotension and maintaining perfusion matter, but the available literature does not support a specific protocol with high-quality evidence; prospective controlled research with validated outcome assessment remains necessary.
